title: the Sri Yantra
hook: a woman on a long flight, her yantra left at home, worships anyway
tomorrow: same brass, same lines. why does one get flowers and one a price tag?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Yantra rose off the page into the Meru, a small mountain where going in is also going up. Today the yantra travels somewhere stranger.

The plane is already climbing when she remembers. The small brass Sri Yantra she worships every morning is still on her altar at home, getting farther away by the minute. No kumkum, no flowers, no lamp, and a long night ahead in a middle seat. The man beside her has his headphones on. At her usual hour, she sets down the tray table, rests her hands in her lap, and closes her eyes. Her lips start to move. Whatever she's looking at, it isn't on the plane.
screen: `THE YANTRA IS STILL ON THE ALTAR.` → `NO FLOWERS, NO LAMP.` → `SHE CLOSES HER EYES ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: What she's looking at is the yantra, held somewhere no suitcase can lose it. A short Sanskrit text called the Bhavana Upanishad teaches exactly this move. Bhavana means contemplation: holding something steady in the mind. The text belongs to Sri Vidya, the worship of the Goddess through the Sri Yantra, and it works like a key. It takes the parts of the diagram, the layers of these past days, and lines them up with parts of a person: the body, the senses, the mind. Then it does the same with worship. Nothing is carried to a plate. The flowers and the lamp become acts of attention, each one offered where the diagram places it. So the road traced on brass becomes a road through the one who sits there. Here's the part worth telling a friend tonight: in this text the worshipper isn't only looking at the map. The worshipper is the map. That doesn't make the brass plate useless. In Sri Vidya some practitioners worship outwardly, some inwardly, some both, and lineages weigh them differently. The woman on the plane will light her lamp again when she lands. And her trick opens the door the next days walk through: a map of the body, drawn for the mind.
screen: `BHAVANA: HOLDING IT IN MIND.` · `THE DIAGRAM, LINED UP WITH A PERSON.` · `WORSHIP AS ATTENTION.` · then, large: `THE WORSHIPPER IS THE MAP.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and close your eyes. Let your attention take in your whole body at once, from where you touch the seat up to the crown of your head, and hold it there as one steady shape. If you pray, you can offer that stillness to the Goddess; if not, simply rest inside it.
The Sri Yantra: the Goddess's diagram, which the Bhavana Upanishad reads onto the worshipper's own body, senses and mind.
Your line: the Sri Yantra, carried where no suitcase and no plate can go. See you tomorrow, wherever you are.

fork.setup: a friend's grandmother can't sit at her home altar for a few weeks after surgery, and she's upset about missing her worship. what does today's idea offer her?
options: worship can also be done in contemplation, with the diagram held within.

fork.reveal: the Bhavana Upanishad treats worship as contemplation too. it doesn't throw out the altar; some do both, and she can light her lamp again when she's well.
